name: Exponentiation II
description: Efficiently compute a^(b^c) mod 1e9+7 for many triples (a, b, c), with the convention 0^0 = 1.
why_hard: The outer exponent b^c is astronomically large, so it must be reduced modulo (p-1) via Fermat's little theorem before the outer fast exponentiation — and the 0^0 = 1 convention plus the case a ≡ 0 (mod p) create edge cases that trip up a naive Euler-theorem application.

name: Multipliers
description: Given n, compute the product of all of its divisors, modulo 1e9+7.
why_hard: Divisors pair up as (d, n/d) with product n, so the answer is n raised to (number of divisors)/2 — but that count can be odd (perfect squares) and n itself can be ≡ 0 mod p, forcing careful modular-exponentiation bookkeeping rather than a naive product loop.

name: Sum of Divisors
description: Compute the sum of σ(i) (sum-of-divisors function) for i = 1..n, modulo 1e9+7, for n up to 10^12.
why_hard: n is too large to sieve directly, so the sum must be rewritten as Σ d·⌊n/d⌋ and evaluated in O(√n) using the floor-division block technique — a step beyond a basic sieve, testing whether the solver knows the divisor-summation identity.

name: Steps to One
description: Starting from an array, repeatedly replace it with a uniformly random non-empty subset and take the GCD of the remaining elements until it becomes 1; find the expected number of steps.
why_hard: Requires computing, for every x, the probability that a random subset's GCD is a multiple of x by counting multiples of x in the array, then sieving downward from large x to small x (Möbius-style subtraction of multiples) to get the exact-GCD-x probabilities before assembling the expectation.

name: Next Prime
description: For up to 20 queries, each giving n up to 10^12, output the smallest prime strictly greater than n.
why_hard: Trial division up to √n (≈10^6) per candidate, repeated across the average prime gap and multiple queries, is too slow within the time limit — the intended solution needs a fast deterministic primality test (Miller–Rabin) to check each candidate in O(log^3 n).

name: Binomial Coefficients
description: Answer many queries of the form "compute C(a, b) mod 1e9+7."
why_hard: With up to 10^5 queries and a, b up to 10^6, per-query computation is too slow — it forces precomputing factorials and modular inverse factorials (via Fermat's little theorem) up front to answer each query in O(1).

name: Anton and School - 2
description: Given a bracket string, for each query range count the number of ways to pick a balanced-bracket subsequence (as a sum over k of C(opens, k)·C(closes, k)).
why_hard: Naively summing C(opens, k)·C(closes, k) over all k is too slow per query; the fast solution collapses the sum into a single binomial coefficient via a Vandermonde-style identity, requiring genuine combinatorial-identity manipulation on top of routine modular nCr.

name: Prime Multiples
description: Given up to 20 distinct primes and n up to 10^18, count how many integers in [1, n] are divisible by at least one of the given primes.
why_hard: With n up to 10^18, only inclusion-exclusion over the 2^20 subsets of the given primes (each subset contributing ⌊n / product⌋) is fast enough — a clean, large-scale test of the inclusion-exclusion principle itself.

name: Unusual Sequences
description: Count the number of sequences of positive integers of any length whose GCD is exactly x and whose elements sum to y.
why_hard: First requires solving "count sequences with GCD exactly 1" via a stars-and-bars-style recurrence, then extending to "GCD exactly x" via a Möbius-function inclusion-exclusion over the multiples of x — a two-layer combination of combinatorics and number theory rather than a single-step formula.

name: Remainders Game
description: Given k and a set of moduli c_1..c_n, decide whether knowing x mod c_i for all i always determines x mod k for every possible x.
why_hard: Forces you to reason about CRT existence/uniqueness conditions (lcm of the c_i vs. k) rather than just running the algorithm.

name: Congruence Equation
description: Given a, b, prime p and bound x, count integers y in [1, x] such that a^y ≡ b (mod p).
why_hard: Combines discrete logarithm / multiplicative order with CRT-style periodic counting to combine residues across the full range.

name: Two Chandeliers
description: Two chandeliers cycle through colors with different periods; find the day of the k-th day their colors differ, using CRT to count matching days up to a bound.
why_hard: Requires binary search over CRT-derived periodicity plus careful inclusion-exclusion on the merged cycle length (lcm of the two periods).

name: Power Tower
description: Compute a power tower w_l^(w_{l+1}^(...)) mod m for range queries, using the generalized Euler theorem (which itself needs CRT-style modulus factoring via repeated totient reduction).
why_hard: Classic "CRT + Euler's theorem tower" problem; the recursive modulus-halving argument is a staple hard-NT technique.

name: ConstructOR
description: Find x < 2^60 such that a|x and b|x (bitwise OR) are both divisible by d, by reasoning over coprime bit-parity constraints reminiscent of CRT-style constraint splitting.
why_hard: Good constructive-CRT-flavored problem for the "combine independent modular/bitwise constraints" mindset, verified via CF API tag `chinese remainder theorem`.

name: Magic Gems
description: Count configurations summing to N units where each magic gem takes 1 unit or is split into M units, for N up to 1e18 — the count follows f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-M).
why_hard: Textbook "derive an order-M linear recurrence then matrix-exponentiate it" problem, a clean step beyond plain Fibonacci.

name: Lunar New Year and a Recursive Sequence
description: Given f_i = (f_{i-1}^{b1} · ... · f_{i-k}^{bk}) mod p for a prime p, find f_n.
why_hard: The recurrence is multiplicative, so you must exponentiate the *exponent vector* via matrix power and separately handle the base via a primitive root / discrete logarithm — a genuinely harder combination than a linear additive recurrence.

name: Fibonotci
description: Compute F_n for a Fibonacci-like recurrence F_n = s_{n-1}F_{n-1} + s_{n-2}F_{n-2} where s is an "almost cyclic" coefficient sequence with a handful of exceptions, over huge n and many queries.
why_hard: Needs precomputed matrix products over one full cycle plus careful patching for the exceptional positions — a much harder generalization of Fibonacci-by-matrix-power.

name: Throwing Dice
description: Count the number of ways to reach sum n by repeatedly throwing a die (1..6), for n up to 10^18.
why_hard: Canonical order-6 linear recurrence that is intractable by plain DP once n exceeds ~10^7, forcing matrix exponentiation.

name: Ceizenpok's formula
difficulty: No CF contest rating (ICPC Gym problem); constraints (n ≤ 1e18, m ≤ 1e6 arbitrary) put it solidly at Div.1 E/hard-2400+ equivalent difficulty
description: Compute C(n, k) mod m for n up to 1e18, k ≤ n, and an *arbitrary* modulus m ≤ 1e6 (not necessarily prime).
why_hard: The canonical "generalized Lucas' theorem" problem — factor m into prime powers via CRT, apply Lucas/Andrew Granville's extension for each prime power, then recombine with CRT. Verified by direct fetch (statement confirms exact n/k/m bounds); note this is the one genuinely well-known Lucas' theorem problem found on a Codeforces-hosted judge — standalone (non-gym) CF/CSES problems requiring pure Lucas' theorem are very rare (see summary).

name: Coprime Subsequences
description: Count the number of subsequences of an array whose gcd is 1.
why_hard: Requires inclusion-exclusion via the Möbius function over multiples to avoid double counting non-coprime subsequences.

name: Make It One
description: Find the minimum-size subset of an array whose gcd is 1, using Möbius-function-weighted subset-sum DP.
why_hard: Combines Möbius inversion with a nontrivial DP bound proof (answer ≤ 7) — a favorite "hard Möbius" problem in most curated lists.

name: Alex and a TV Show
description: Support union/gcd/lcm updates on multisets and answer "count of x with a given gcd" queries via randomization plus a Möbius-transform-style array.
why_hard: Rare combination of Möbius/divisor-transform ideas with randomized hashing for online updates.

name: Counting Coprime Pairs
description: Given n integers up to 10^6, count the number of pairs that are coprime.
why_hard: The standard entry-level-but-still-nontrivial Möbius sieve counting problem — a clean verification target before tackling 803F/1043F.

name: Kuroni and Impossible Calculation
description: Given n integers and a modulus m, compute the product of |a_i − a_j| over every pair i < j, modulo m.
why_hard: With n up to 2·10^5, only pigeonhole rescues the problem: since m ≤ 1000, once n > m two elements must share the same residue mod m, forcing some factor — and hence the whole product — to be 0 mod m; spotting that early-exit is the entire solution, since below it the array is small enough to brute-force the O(n^2) product directly.

name: Bear and Prime Numbers
description: Given up to 10^6 integers (each ≤ 10^7) and up to 5·10^4 queries [l, r], answer for each query the sum over every prime p in [l, r] of how many array elements are divisible by p.
why_hard: Query bounds run up to 2·10^9, but no array value can have a prime factor above 10^7, so the trick is to build a sieve-based prime-divisor-count array only up to 10^7, prefix-sum it once, and clamp every query's upper bound to 10^7 — missing that clamp is the classic trap that blows up a naive per-query sieve.

name: Count GCD
description: Given an array a of length n (values ≤ m), count arrays b of the same length and bound such that gcd(b_1, ..., b_i) = a_i for every prefix i, modulo 998244353.
why_hard: First requires the existence check that a_i must divide a_{i-1}; then, writing b_i = a_i·c_i, each step reduces to counting values of c_i up to a_{i-1}/a_i that are coprime to a_{i-1}/a_i — an Euler-totient-style count computed via a precomputed smallest-prime-factor sieve rather than one direct closed-form.

name: Almost Identity Permutations
description: Given n (≤1000) and k (≤4), count permutations of 1..n in which at least n−k indices satisfy p_i = i.
why_hard: The count is a sum over j = 0..k of C(n, j) times D(j), the number of derangements of j elements — the real insight is that k ≤ 4 means only the derangement counts 0,1,2,9,44 are ever needed, turning what looks like a general inclusion-exclusion derivation into a five-case lookup.

name: Modular Stability
description: Given n and k, count strictly increasing arrays 1 ≤ a_1 < ... < a_k ≤ n such that x mod a_1 mod a_2 ... mod a_k gives the same value no matter what order the a_i are applied in, for every non-negative integer x, modulo 998244353.
why_hard: The permutation-invariance condition on nested mod operations collapses, after careful case analysis, to a single surprising arithmetic fact: only the smallest chosen element a_1 must divide every other element — turning the count into 'for each candidate smallest divisor d, choose the rest freely from its multiples up to n,' summed efficiently over all d.
